background.definition: Decompression sickness (DCS) is a multisystem condition resulting from nitrogen bubble formation in veins and tissues due to a decrease in ambient pressure. Type I DCS, the less severe form, is characterized by musculoskeletal, cutaneous, and lymphatic symptoms, along with general symptoms such as malaise, anorexia, and fatigue. Type II DCS, the more severe form, includes pulmonary and neurological symptoms, hemoconcentration, and hypovolemic shock. Ambient pressure is the pressure of the surrounding environment exerted on an individual at a given location. It varies depending on altitude, depth, and surrounding conditions, and it influences how gases behave in the body, especially during activities such as diving or flying.

list.listitem: The incidence of decompression illness, encompassing both DCS and arterial gas embolism, is approximately 4 cases per 10,000 exposures in recreational divers.
The incidence per dive of DCS in recreational scuba divers ranges from 0.90 to 5 in 10,000.

The etiology of DCS lies in decompression, which can result from a reduction in ambient pressure following exposure to elevated pressure environments. This decompression can occur either when moving from atmospheric pressure to a lower pressure at high altitude (as in aviators), or when transitioning from a raised ambient pressure back to atmospheric pressure (as in divers or workers in compressed air environments). In both cases, the rapid decrease in pressure causes nitrogen gas, dissolved under higher pressure, to form bubbles within the body’s tissues and bloodstream, leading to the symptoms characteristic of DCS.
When breathing air (which is nitrogen-rich), body tissues gradually absorb nitrogen until they reach nitrogen saturation.
Inert gases like nitrogen can dissolve in body fluids depending on ambient pressure and temperature, entering a liquid phase under higher pressures.
During ascent, as ambient pressure decreases, dissolved nitrogen transitions from a liquid to a gas, forming bubbles.

With a gradual reduction in ambient pressure, the body can safely expel nitrogen by passively transferring it down a concentration gradient: from tissues to the blood, and eventually through the lungs.
The lungs have a maximum rate at which they can eliminate nitrogen; rapid ascent can exceed this rate, leading to nitrogen supersaturation in tissues.
If nitrogen elimination is overwhelmed, gas bubbles can form, potentially causing tissue compression and, in some cases, embolization within blood vessels, resulting in decompression sickness.

list.listitem: DCS manifestations depend on the organs affected, with presentations ranging from skin itching and vague constitutional symptoms to shock and cardiopulmonary arrest.

Type I DCS typically presents as deep, aching, poorly localized musculoskeletal pain, varying from mild to severe. Symptoms usually begin within 1 hour of resurfacing and may progressively worsen over the next 24 to 36 hours..

Type II DCS presents with neurological symptoms, which can range from numbness, tingling, and paresthesias to paraplegia or permanent nerve damage due to spinal cord injury. Neurological symptoms generally appear about 60 minutes after surfacing, occurring in approximately 88% of divers..
Type II may also present with cardiorespiratory symptoms, including retrosternal discomfort, cough, and dyspnea.

Risk factors that increase the likelihood of DCS include the maximum depth of the last dive, complete relief of symptoms following initial recompression, fine cerebellar signs as secondary symptoms, a missed decompression stop in a recent dive, and a history of prior DCS.

Conversely, primary presenting symptoms such as seizures or pulmonary complaints, along with a delayed symptom onset of more than 2 to 3 hours after resurfacing, are negative predictive factors for DCS.

The risk of severe DCS (Type II) is more than doubled in divers with a patent foramen ovale (PFO), regardless of whether they are recreational, commercial, or military divers, with an odds ratio of 2.52 (95% CI, 1.5-4.25; P < .001) compared to those without a PFO.

Among 100 experienced divers followed over an average of 28.7 months, the incidence of DCI was 8.4 per 10,000 person-dives in those with high-risk PFOs, 2 per 10,000 in those with low-risk PFOs, and 0 in those without PFOs (OR 9.34 for high-risk PFO vs. no PFO).
Imaging studies like CT and MRI are less sensitive than clinical evaluation for diagnosis of DCS, and its use frequently serves only to delay appropriate treatment.
Using CT scanning compared to post-mortem examination, pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema and intraarterial gas have been found to be nonspecific for decompression illness.
A chest x-ray may be indicated if there is concern for a pneumothorax, since this must be treated before recompression therapy.
Laboratory testing is only useful to assess for hemoconcentration, dehydration and drug use.

Clinical evidence is lacking for the use of corticosteroids, anticoagulants and lidocaine for DCS treatment.

Early administration of supplemental oxygen, with a concentration as close to 100%, improves clinical outcome. A fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) of 100% can best be accomplished by tracheal intubation.
IV hydration with isotonic fluids without glucose is recommended to treat dehydration and increase the washout of gases.

Definitive treatment is recompression in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber at sea level. The most commonly used treatment algorithm, also referred to as tables, are the US Navy Tables 5 and 6. The latter consists of three pure oxygen 20 minutes cycles at 18 m of sea water (.28 MPa) followed by oxygen cycles at 9 msw (.19 MPa), with intermittent 5 minutes air breathing pauses.

There is evidence from a single small randomized trial with 41 patients that a shorter chamber treatment table is more effective for persons with mild DCS. The shorter treatment table (Fremantle Hospital 01) was more likely to result in complete symptom resolution after the initial treatment (17/20 vs 8/21, p = 0.003). C
The head-down position (Trendelenburg) is no longer recommended except for the treatment of hypotension.
Outcome is significantly worsened by hyperthermia, so body temperature should be closely monitored in patients with DCS.
Adequate initial therapy is thought to improve clinical outcomes. C
Long-term follow-up studies have shown that residual inner ear damage is common following inner ear DCS. B
